posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-score post from a CRO with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain with a specific observation about explainability being the real blocker, not AI itself
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is the one that ends careers in regulated industries. It's not really an AI problem — it's an audit trail problem. The output might be right, but if you can't walk a regulator back through the logic step by step, the number is worthless. Curious how your team is thinking about what 'explainable enough' actually looks like in practice?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the real problem (trust, not tooling) and add a sharp insight about why dashboards lose to Excel every time
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the problem. Excel wins because everyone knows where the numbers came from — someone they trust ran a formula they can trace. Dashboards ask people to just... believe. And that's a completely different ask than 'here's a better chart'. What did your finance team say when you asked them why they didn't trust it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add a layer on why it happens structurally, leave her thinking
posts.draft_comment: The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells the whole story. Most dashboards get built to answer 'what could we track?' instead of 'what do we actually decide?' — and once you've added 47 metrics, nobody has the political will to cut them. Curious what the pushback was internally when you made the call to gut it.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post that nails the semantic layer problem — validate the 'who owns truth' framing and add the insight that tooling is never the bottleneck, definitions are
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. Everyone gets access, builds their own version of the truth, and suddenly 'revenue' means four different things depending on which dashboard your CFO opened this morning. The tool was never the hard bit — it's the unglamorous work of getting finance, ops, and product to agree on a single definition before anyone writes a query. Wonder how many orgs actually solve that before they buy the licenses.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucinations as a security risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the framing, add the specific trust layer that's missing in most analytics tools
posts.draft_comment: The 'treat outputs like inputs' framing is sharp — most analytics teams still haven't caught up to that. The problem I keep seeing is that AI-generated numbers arrive with the same visual confidence as verified data. No audit trail, no sourcing, no way to know what the model actually touched. How do you think about establishing chain of custody for an AI-generated insight the same way you would for a user action?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect Helen Cross (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging on a post about BI tools failing business users — validate the pain with a specific observation, add the hidden reason most people miss
posts.draft_comment: The £200k thing happens more than vendors would ever admit. The dirty secret is most of these tools were designed to impress in a demo — not to be picked up cold by a head of ops on a Tuesday afternoon with no data background. So the power user becomes the bottleneck, and suddenly 'self-service' just means 'one person does it themselves'. What would it even look like to test for that before you sign?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at an industrial company surfacing a data trust problem that's really a process/ownership problem — validate the root cause diagnosis, add the layer about what actually breaks trust in BI.
posts.draft_comment: The filter thing is almost never the real problem — it's that nobody agreed whose version of the number was official before anyone built the dashboard. Culture is right, but I'd go one level deeper: it's about ownership. Who owns the definition of 'revenue this quarter'? Until that's a named person with a documented answer, the filters will keep drifting. Does Oakwood have anyone who actually owns that, or does it fall to whoever built the report?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' problem — validate the adoption gap insight and reframe it as a data literacy issue, not a tool issue
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is painfully honest. Most rollouts die the same way — the tool works fine, but people don't have enough context about their own data to know what question is even worth asking. Shadow AI on personal phones is just people finding the path of least resistance. The real gap isn't access, it's confidence.
